title: Karl Marx
orientation: Russell treats Marx purely as a philosopher and as an influence on other philosophers, deliberately setting aside Marx's economics and most of his politics. He presents Marx as a genuinely hard case to classify -- part heir to the Philosophical Radicals' rationalism, part revivifier of materialism in a new 'dialectical' and quasi-instrumentalist sense, and part last of the great Hegelian system-builders -- and uses the chapter to test, and partly to endorse, Marx's own central thesis that philosophies are shaped by their social and economic circumstances.
historical_background: Marx was born in 1818 at Trier into a family of former rabbis who had converted to Christianity; he studied under still-dominant Hegelianism and Feuerbach's materialist revolt against it, edited the radical Rheinische Zeitung until it was suppressed, went to France in 1843 to study Socialism, met Engels (a Manchester factory manager) and through him learned English labour conditions and economics, took part in the 1848 revolutions, and then spent most of the rest of his life in poverty and illness in London. Russell is writing in 1943, noting that Marxist parties had by then either moderated (Weimar Germany's Social Democrats), been suppressed (Nazi Germany), or taken power outright (the Soviet Union).
philosophical_problems: Can a philosopher's doctrines be explained away entirely as products of his social and economic position, or are some philosophical questions genuinely independent of social causation?
What does it mean to replace 'passive' sensation with an 'activist' or 'instrumentalist' theory of knowledge, in which subject and object mutually transform each other?
Can Hegel's dialectical logic of historical development be detached from his idealist metaphysics and re-grounded in matter and economic production?
Is progress a universal law, and can ethical considerations be dispensed with if a historical outcome is believed to be inevitable?

How should the historian of philosophy weigh purely technical, quasi-scientific progress in philosophy (e.g., on universals or the ontological argument) against philosophy understood as an 'organic whole of extra-rational decisions'?

philosophers_discussed.name: Karl Marx
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented in three intertwined aspects: heir to the Philosophical Radicals' rationalism and anti-romanticism; a 'dialectical materialist' who reinterprets sensation as an active, practical process rather than passive contemplation; and the last great Hegelian system-builder, who replaces Hegel's Spirit with matter (in practice, economics) as history's driving force via the materialist conception of history.

philosophers_discussed.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The philosopher whose dialectical logic and belief in a rational formula summing up the evolution of mankind Marx inherits and inverts, substituting matter/classes for Hegel's mystical 'Spirit'/nations as the moving force of history.

philosophers_discussed.name: Ludwig Feuerbach
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited with the materialist revolt against Hegel that influenced the young Marx at university, and as the addressee of Marx's 1845 Theses on Feuerbach, quoted by Russell on the practical, non-purely-theoretical nature of truth.

philosophers_discussed.name: Friedrich Engels
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Marx's collaborator, a Manchester factory manager through whom Marx gained direct knowledge of English labour conditions and economics.

schools_discussed: Hegelian dialectic (as inherited and transformed by Marx)
Marxism as a modern political-philosophical movement
Fascism/Nazism, discussed by contrast as the third, anti-rational strand of modern politics

core_concepts.name: Dialectical materialism (activist theory of knowledge)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Instead of thinking of knowing as a passive mind simply receiving impressions from a fixed outside world, Marx thought that knowing is a kind of doing: the knower and the thing known constantly reshape each other through practical activity, rather like using and thereby altering a tool.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Marx's 'dialectical' materialism, distinct from eighteenth-century materialism, holds that sensation or perception is an interaction between subject and object in which the object, apart from the activity of the percipient, is mere raw material transformed in the process of being known; truth is therefore demonstrated in practice, not established by isolated contemplation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell says Marx was, so far as he knows, the first philosopher to criticize the notion of 'truth' from this activist standpoint, anticipating instrumentalist and pragmatist theories of knowledge discussed in the following chapters.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed under Hegelian influence and in reaction against both traditional (passive) materialism and idealism; stated in the 1845 Theses on Feuerbach.
examples: Marx's Thesis: 'The question whether objective truth belongs to human thinking is not a question of theory, but a practical question... Philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways, but the real task is to alter it.'
competing_positions: Traditional materialism, which regarded sensation as passive and attributed activity primarily to the object
British empiricism's notion of passive 'sensation,' which Marx's view denies, preferring 'noticing' (which implies activity)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell links it to 'what is now called instrumentalism,' anticipating the discussion of William James and John Dewey in the chapters that follow.

core_concepts.name: The materialist conception of history
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The idea that a society's politics, religion, philosophy, and art are, in their broad outlines, products of how that society produces and distributes goods -- so that to understand a period's ideas you must first understand its economic structure.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Marx's doctrine that the politics, religion, philosophy, and art of any historical epoch are, in their broad outlines (though not in every technical detail), an outcome of its methods of production and, to a lesser extent, distribution.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this 'a very important thesis,' says it concerns the historian of philosophy directly, and admits it has influenced his own view of philosophical development as presented throughout this book, even though he does not accept it as it stands.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Marx's synthesis of Hegelian dialectic with British classical economics, substituting matter (in practice, economics) for Hegel's Spirit as history's motive force.
examples: Greek philosophy to Aristotle expressing the mentality of the City State
Stoicism as appropriate to cosmopolitan despotism
Scholastic philosophy as the intellectual expression of the Church as an organization
Philosophy since Locke embodying the prejudices of the commercial middle class
Marxism and Fascism as philosophies appropriate to the modern industrial State
objections: Russell's first objection: social causation is as much political (a matter of power) as economic (a matter of wealth); wealth is only one form of power.

Russell's second objection: social causation largely ceases to apply once a philosophical problem becomes sufficiently detailed and technical (e.g., the classical debate over universals, or the fate of the ontological argument).
competing_positions: Russell's own view that 'philosophy' in the strict, technical sense (logic, mathematics, precise conceptual analysis) is largely insulated from social causation, while 'philosophy' as an 'organic whole of extra-rational decisions' is where Marx's thesis is largely true
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell states outright that it has influenced his own account of philosophical development throughout A History of Western Philosophy.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to Marx's whole account of the relation between economics, politics, and ideas.

core_concepts.name: The dialectic of feudalism, capitalism, and Socialism (classes replacing nations)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Marx borrowed Hegel's three-step pattern of historical development but changed its subject: instead of nations acting out a mystical Spirit's logic, it is economic classes (landowners, industrial employers, wage-earners) that move history forward toward Socialism.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Marx's substitution of a single historical triad -- feudalism (the landowner), capitalism (the industrial employer), and Socialism (the wage-earner) -- and of classes for Hegel's nations, as the vehicles of an inevitable, deterministic dialectical movement.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It gave Marx's Socialism the appearance of scientific inevitability (a prophecy, not merely an ethical preference), while, Russell argues, quietly smuggling in an unexamined belief in progress that only theism could really justify.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Adapted from Hegel's philosophy of history as expressed in the Logic.
objections: Russell notes Marx disclaimed ethical or humanitarian grounds for preferring Socialism, calling it merely the side taken by the deterministic dialectic -- yet Russell judges this only partly true, since Marx clearly also believed Socialism would increase human happiness.
competing_positions: Hegel's own version, in which 'Spirit,' not matter, drives historical development through nations rather than classes
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped the Social Democratic Party's programme in Germany and, in a more fanatical form, the government of Soviet Russia.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: frames the modern division between Liberals, Marxists, and Fascists/Nazis.

core_concepts.name: Marx's uncritical nineteenth-century belief in inevitable progress
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Like most people of his century, Marx assumed history was moving in a generally upward direction, which let him treat the coming of Socialism as automatically an improvement without needing to argue for it on ethical grounds.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis that Marx's confinement of philosophical purview to Man on this one planet, combined with a Copernican failure to register humanity's lack of cosmic importance, produced an unexamined readiness to believe in progress as a universal law, allowing him to dispense with ethics: 'If Socialism was coming, it must be an improvement.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as Marx's gravest philosophical shortcoming: an atheist who nonetheless 'retained a cosmic optimism which only theism could justify.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: A characteristic assumption of nineteenth-century thought generally, shared by Marx's contemporaries.
objections: Russell: 'Broadly speaking, all the elements in Marx's philosophy which are derived from Hegel are unscientific, in the sense that there is no reason whatever to suppose them true.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Bears on the relation between Marx's professed atheism and his implicit quasi-religious optimism.

arguments.title: Marx's argument for the materialist conception of history
premises: The 'driving force' of historical development, for Marx, is matter understood specifically as man's relation to matter -- above all his mode of production.
The politics, religion, philosophy, and art of any epoch are outcomes, in their broad outlines, of that epoch's methods of production and distribution.
arguments.conclusion: History develops according to a dialectical formula whose motive force is economic (the materialist conception of history), not Hegel's mystical Spirit.
arguments.explanation: Russell partially accepts this thesis as containing 'very important elements of truth' and admits its influence on his own historical method, while insisting it needs qualifying rather than accepting wholesale.
objections: Social causation is as much political (power) as economic (wealth).

Social causation largely ceases to apply once a problem becomes sufficiently detailed and technical, as shown by the history of the problem of universals and of the ontological argument, where genuine, non-ideological progress has occurred.
implications: If accepted only in Russell's qualified form, philosophy divides into a technical, quasi-scientific part relatively free of social causation, and a broader 'organic whole of extra-rational decisions' that is genuinely shaped by social forces (including, but not limited to, economics).

arguments.title: Russell's case study of the ontological argument against strict Marxist determinism
premises: The ontological argument was invented by Anselm, rejected by Aquinas, accepted by Descartes, refuted by Kant, and reinstated by Hegel -- a sequence spanning many different social and economic contexts.
Modern logical analysis of the concept of 'existence' has, as a purely technical matter, proved the argument invalid.
arguments.conclusion: The refutation of the ontological argument is a technical, logical achievement, not an outcome explainable by reference to the social system of any particular thinker.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses this history to show that some philosophical questions can be settled (or shown insoluble) by purely technical progress, independent of the economic interests Marx's theory would invoke.
implications: Refuting the ontological argument gives no ground for supposing its conclusion (God's existence) false, since even Aquinas, a believer, rejected the argument.

arguments.title: Russell's argument that Marx smuggled in an unjustified belief in progress
premises: Marx confined his philosophical horizon to Man on this planet, without assimilating the post-Copernican fact that Man lacks cosmic importance.
This terrestrial confinement went with a nineteenth-century readiness to believe progress is a universal law.
Only this unexamined belief in inevitable progress let Marx treat the coming of Socialism as necessarily an improvement, dispensing with the need for independent ethical argument.
arguments.conclusion: Marx, though professing atheism, in fact retained 'a cosmic optimism which only theism could justify,' and the Hegelian elements of his philosophy are, in Russell's judgment, unscientific.
arguments.explanation: This is Russell's central overall verdict on Marx as 'considered purely as a philosopher,' distinguishing the philosophically weak Hegelian trappings from what Russell considers Marx's genuinely important, non-philosophical, sociological observations about industrial capitalism.
implications: Russell suggests the Hegelian dialectical apparatus could be 'dropped with advantage,' leaving Marx's substantive claims about industrial cruelty, monopoly, and the inevitability of proletarian revolt intact as claims for economics and politics to evaluate, not philosophy.

key_distinctions: The materialist conception of history as applied to 'philosophy' in the broad, extra-rational sense vs. to narrowly technical/logical philosophical problems
Hegel's 'Spirit' driving nations vs. Marx's matter (economics) driving classes
Prophecy (a deterministic prediction) vs. advocacy (an ethical recommendation) -- the ambiguity Russell finds in Marx's stance toward Socialism
The subjective sense in which every philosopher believes himself to pursue objective truth vs. the objective, socially conditioned reality of many philosophers' unconscious biases
Liberals, Marxists, and Fascists/Nazis as the three modern political-philosophical camps, the first two broadly rationalist and empirical, the third anti-rational and will-centered
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Marx is presented as simultaneously an outcome of the Philosophical Radicals (like Hodgskin, continuing their rationalism and opposition to Romanticism), a revivifier of eighteenth-century materialism in a new, 'dialectical' key, and the direct successor to Hegel as a system-builder governed by a rational formula summing up the evolution of mankind. Russell also traces Marx's economics back to British classical economics (which Marx reoriented from serving the capitalist to serving the wage-earner).
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell explicitly links Marx's activist theory of truth to 'what is now called instrumentalism,' directly anticipating the treatment of William James's pragmatism and John Dewey's instrumentalism in the two chapters that follow. He also situates Marxism, in Russell's own historical moment (1943), as one of three rival modern ideological-philosophical camps, alongside Liberalism and Fascism/Nazism (traced to Rousseau, Fichte, and Nietzsche).
political_social_context: Marx's doctrines shaped the German Social Democratic Party (winning a third of votes cast in the 1912 election), briefly held power in the early Weimar Republic (Ebert), had by Russell's time of writing (1943) become the state ideology of the Soviet Union, remained absent from mainstream Western labour movements (the British Labour Party stayed empirically socialist rather than Marxist), gained wide influence among Western intellectuals, and had been forcibly suppressed under the Nazis in Germany.
religion_science_culture_context: Marx professed atheism but, in Russell's reading, retained an essentially religious cosmic optimism about the inevitability of progress; Russell also situates Marx's materialism against the post-Copernican scientific reordering of humanity's cosmic significance.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Marx as a genuinely three-sided figure -- rationalist heir of the Philosophical Radicals, innovator of an 'activist' materialism anticipating instrumentalism, and last great Hegelian system-builder -- who is hard to reduce to any single label. He credits Marx's materialist conception of history with real, partly-accepted insight (acknowledging its influence on his own historiographical method in this book), while offering two explicit objections: social causation is as much political as economic, and it largely ceases to apply to technical philosophical questions once they become sufficiently detailed (illustrated via the problem of universals and the ontological argument). Russell's overall philosophical verdict is critical: Marx is 'too practical, too much wrapped up in the problems of his time,' fails to assimilate the post-Copernican demotion of Man's cosmic importance, and smuggles in an unscientific, quasi-religious belief in inevitable progress that lets him dispense with ethical argument for Socialism. Russell suggests the substantive, non-Hegelian core of Marx's views on industrial cruelty and the tendency of capitalism toward monopoly could be stated, and perhaps better defended, without the Hegelian dialectical apparatus.
critical_context: Marxist and post-Marxist scholarship has long debated exactly the two objections Russell raises here -- that Marxian base/superstructure explanation neglects the autonomy of political power, and that it strains to account for technical, cumulative progress in fields like logic and mathematics; twentieth-century Western Marxists (e.g., the Frankfurt School) developed more nuanced accounts of ideology precisely to address such objections, though a full survey of that literature is outside the scope of Russell's chapter.
key_takeaways: Russell examines Marx purely as a philosopher, deliberately excluding his economics and most of his practical politics from evaluation.
Marx's 'dialectical' materialism treats knowing as an active, practical interaction between subject and object, not passive contemplation -- Russell links this to later instrumentalism.

The materialist conception of history holds that a period's politics, religion, philosophy, and art broadly reflect its methods of production; Russell partly accepts this but raises two objections: power is not reducible to wealth, and technical philosophical problems can be resolved independently of social causation.
Marx replaces Hegel's mystical 'Spirit' driving nations with matter (in practice, economics) driving classes through a feudalism-capitalism-Socialism dialectic.

Russell's chief philosophical criticism is that Marx, though an avowed atheist, relied on an unexamined nineteenth-century belief in inevitable progress to treat Socialism as necessarily an improvement, without independent ethical argument.

Russell suggests Marx's substantive sociological claims (industrial cruelty, tendency toward monopoly, inevitability of proletarian revolt) could be stated, and might stand or fall, without the Hegelian dialectical framework.
study_notes:
This chapter is best read as a test case for the materialist conception of history itself -- Russell uses Marx's own theory to examine Marx. Notice the two-part structure: first, an exposition of what makes Marx a genuinely hybrid figure (rationalist Radical, activist materialist, Hegelian system-builder); second, a sustained critical engagement with Marx's central historiographical claim. Russell's own qualified acceptance is important to track carefully -- he says the materialist conception of history is 'both true and important' at a broad level (e.g., explaining why Greek philosophy fits the City State, or scholasticism fits the Church), but he draws a sharp line once a problem becomes technical: the resolution of the ontological argument, or the modern near-resolution of the ancient problem of universals, are, in his view, achievements of logic, not by-products of economic interest. 

Also pay attention to Russell's diagnosis of Marx's 'cosmic optimism': this is not a claim about Marx's economics but about an unexamined metaphysical assumption -- that progress is inevitable -- which lets an ethical question (should we want Socialism?) collapse into a merely predictive one (is Socialism coming?). This same move, treating what 'will happen' as settling what 'ought to happen,' recurs as a pattern Russell criticizes across several chapters in this Part (compare his critique of Hegel and of J. S. Mill's utilitarian 'proof' in the previous chapter).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Marx's view that knowing the world is not passive observation but an active, practical process in which the knower and the world shape each other.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Marx's reinterpretation of materialism, under Hegelian influence, holding that sensation is an interaction between subject and object rather than passive contemplation, and that truth is demonstrated in practice rather than by isolated theoretical reflection.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that a society's ideas, religion, art, and politics are largely shaped by how it produces and distributes goods.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Marx's doctrine that the politics, religion, philosophy, and art of an epoch are, in broad outline, an outcome of its methods of production and distribution, replacing Hegel's Spirit-driven history with an economically driven one.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A pattern of historical change in stages, where each stage produces tensions that push society into the next stage -- for Marx, feudalism to capitalism to Socialism.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Marx's adaptation of Hegel's dialectical logic of historical development, substituting classes (landowner, industrial employer, wage-earner) for Hegel's nations as the vehicles of an inevitable, deterministic historical movement.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A short 1845 text by Marx arguing that philosophy's real job is to change the world, not just interpret it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Marx's eleven theses (1845) criticizing Feuerbach's contemplative materialism and asserting that the reality and power of thought must be demonstrated in practice, culminating in the claim that 'philosophers have only interpreted the world... the real task is to alter it.'

questions.prompt: What three distinct aspects of Marx does Russell identify, and why does he say emphasizing only one gives a distorted view?
questions.answer: Marx is (1) an outcome of the Philosophical Radicals, continuing their rationalism and anti-romanticism; (2) a revivifier of materialism in a new 'dialectical' sense; and (3) the last great Hegelian system-builder, seeking a rational formula for history. Russell says stressing any one alone distorts the picture because Marx's philosophy genuinely combines all three.
questions.explanation: This threefold framing structures the whole chapter and explains why Marx is 'difficult to classify.'

questions.prompt: According to Russell, how does Marx's 'dialectical' materialism differ from older, eighteenth-century materialism?
questions.answer: Older materialism regarded sensation as passive, with activity attributed mainly to the object; Marx held that all perception is an interaction between subject and object, so that the object is mere raw material transformed in the process of being known -- closer to what is now called instrumentalism.
questions.explanation: Russell draws directly on Marx's Theses on Feuerbach to make this point.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's two main objections to Marx's materialist conception of history.
questions.answer: First, social circumstances relevant to a philosophy are as much political (power) as economic (wealth), which is only one form of power. Second, social causation largely stops applying once a problem becomes sufficiently detailed and technical, as shown by the eventual near-resolution of the problem of universals and the definitive refutation of the ontological argument through purely logical analysis.
questions.explanation: Russell illustrates the second objection with concrete case studies from the history of philosophy, distinguishing technical progress from ideologically-driven belief.

questions.prompt: Contrast Hegel's and Marx's accounts of the driving force of history.
questions.answer: Hegel believed a mystical entity called 'Spirit' drives history through the stages of his dialectical Logic, with nations as its vehicles. Marx kept the dialectical, stage-based structure but replaced Spirit with matter -- specifically man's relation to matter, chiefly his mode of production -- and replaced nations with classes (landowner, industrial employer, wage-earner) as history's vehicles.
questions.explanation: This substitution is the technical core of what Marx called turning Hegel's dialectic 'right side up.'

questions.prompt: What does Russell identify as Marx's gravest philosophical shortcoming, considered purely as a philosopher?
questions.answer: That Marx confined his purview to Man on this one planet, failed to assimilate the post-Copernican demotion of Man's cosmic importance, and relied on an unexamined nineteenth-century belief in inevitable progress to treat Socialism's coming as necessarily an improvement -- an atheist retaining 'a cosmic optimism which only theism could justify.'
questions.explanation: This is Russell's strongest and most quoted critical verdict in the chapter.

questions.prompt: What three political-ideological camps does Russell identify in the modern world at the time of writing (1943), and how does he characterize their philosophical relationships to one another?
questions.answer: Liberals (following Locke or Bentham), Marxists (governing Russia), and Nazis/Fascists (tracing to Rousseau, Fichte, and Nietzsche). Russell says Liberals and Marxists, though politically sharply divided, are philosophically not far apart -- both rationalistic, scientific, and empirical in intention -- whereas the third camp differs from the other two 'far more profoundly,' being anti-rational and anti-scientific and centered on will to power.
questions.explanation: This closing framing links the Marx chapter forward to the book's broader argument about the modern crisis of rationalism.

options: Marx's economics and most of his politics

quiz.prompt: Whose materialism, according to Marx, wrongly regarded sensation as passive?
quiz.explanation: Marx contrasted his own 'dialectical' materialism with the older, eighteenth-century sort that treated sensation as passive.

quiz.prompt: What does Marx substitute for Hegel's 'Spirit' as the driving force of history?
options: Matter, in the sense of man's relation to matter, chiefly his mode of production
quiz.explanation: Marx keeps Hegel's dialectical structure but replaces the mystical entity 'Spirit' with matter, which in practice means economics.
quiz.related_concept: The dialectic of feudalism, capitalism, and Socialism (classes replacing nations)

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is one of Russell's two stated objections to the materialist conception of history?
options: That it is entirely untestable and therefore meaningless
That social causation is as much political (power) as economic (wealth)
That Marx never applied it to his own writings
That it contradicts the theory of evolution
quiz.explanation: Russell's first objection is that social circumstances include political power, not merely economic wealth, which he develops further in his book Power.

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that the eventual refutation of the ontological argument by modern logic can be fully explained by the social and economic interests of the philosophers involved.
quiz.explanation: Russell uses the ontological argument's history precisely to show the opposite: its refutation is 'a purely technical matter,' independent of social causation.

That it applies only to feudal societies

quiz.explanation: Hegel supplied the dialectical framework, Feuerbach the materialist reaction against Hegelian idealism, and Engels the practical knowledge of English industrial conditions.
